detail.claimant: Gino Caspari and Agnese Faccini (2025), A Key to the Voynich Manuscript, Table 1 and Figures 1–2. Open preprint: https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3644902_2/component/file_3644903/content

statement: This is the fixed glyph layer of the proposed key. EVA units were aligned with Table 1's glyph images and the Zandbergen–Landini transcription of the authors' addressed examples. In particular, f2r.1–2 gives ypchol → expol, ckholsy → dfolie, dorchory → torpore, chkar → pdn, and shor → fior. For glyphs with alternative outputs, fix ch to P as in torpore, sh to FI as in fior, p to X as in expol, and ckh to DF as in dfolie. Greedy longest-match segmentation treats ar and aiin as single units. Glyphs without a secure EVA alignment are omitted from the map. The test covers this fixed reading layer, with no contextual F/P alternation or conjectural shorthand expansion. The authors give examples of these choices, but no deterministic expansion rule for unseen passages.
title: Gino Caspari and Agnese Faccini (2025), A Key to the Voynich Manuscript, Table 1 and Figures 1–2. Open preprint: https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3644902_2/c

established: In the tested corpus, the preceding token identity explains 0.79% of capped token entropy after shuffle correction, while the last and first glyphs across adjacent tokens share 0.197 bits of shuffle-corrected mutual information.

Uncertain separators have higher cross-boundary cohesion and narrower image-coordinate gaps than certain separators. Manually drawn coordinate boxes distinguished the two classes with AUC 0.905 among matched boundaries. A smaller blind measurement of the ink gave the same direction and weaker discrimination.
After erasing every space before learning the units, the 64-merge segmentation crossed 2.5% of certain and 20.3% of uncertain separators. The direction held in each of the 16 analyzed quires.
Byte-pair merges identify an early multi-symbol scale of reduced adjacent dependence, with a minimum at 32 merges when scored on omitted quires and at 64 in the pooled fit.

The tested Naibbe and self-citation outputs approximate the manuscript's low glyph entropy, early merge scale, weak token order and null substitution-attack differential. Their tested outputs have substantially weaker edge-glyph dependence and fewer singleton types than the manuscript at matched token counts.

open.check: Measure ink-to-ink gap widths blind to the transcription labels, matching the neighboring glyph pair and accounting for page or quire clustering.
open.question: Can the graded separator distinction be reproduced with independently segmented image measurements at manuscript scale?

open.check: At matched token counts and with fixed generator settings, compare shuffle-corrected edge-glyph mutual information and singleton-type fraction jointly against the manuscript and the published controls.
open.question: Can a candidate text-production procedure reproduce both the strong cross-token edge dependence and the singleton-rich vocabulary at the manuscript's sample size?

detail.why: the synthetic text does not reproduce the fact

statement: Layout-blind periodic table text, fitted on public Currier B pages only. Words are drawn independently by frequency from the public Currier B word list; every tenth word (ten being the commonest paragraph line length on the public B pages) is drawn from the words ending in m, all others from the words not ending in m. The writer never sees where a line ends. This is the strongest procedure of its kind I could find: periods 8 to 13 were tried on the practice split and none lifts the line-final to mid-line ratio above about 1.0, against 61.6 for the manuscript there. Sent as a best attempt that does not land: F-001 survives every generator that cannot see the line break. It says nothing about language, though; a writer who can see the line end and puts an m-final word there would reproduce it, and the attack format (a word stream re-cut to the hidden line shapes) cannot express such a rule.
title: fact attack on F-001

detail.authors: Xin Zhang and Victor S. Sheng
established: On the published measure of within-line word-pair replication, the manuscript scored 0.071 in Zandbergen–Landini and 0.053 in Takahashi. The 28 length- and layout-matched natural-text samples in 16 languages scored 0.139–0.411.

The tested copying procedure outperformed the tested single-key ciphers on the held-back statistics. Some two-key and word-class cipher programs performed comparably, and no tested program met the joint check across all 37 statistics.

For the tested fits of a noisy two-key open nomenclator, the solver and frequency checks supported exclusions in 14 of 16 languages. Arabic and Hebrew remained outside those exclusions, and the nomenclator solver also failed to recover its Hebrew positive controls.

open.check: Freeze the solver and evaluate planted-key recovery on independently selected texts at matched layout and noise levels before interpreting manuscript results.
open.question: How much power can a calibrated search obtain against open nomenclators in historical Hebrew and Arabic when planted keys include distinct tables and noisy transcription?

open.check: Use identical line widths and token budgets in synthetic and manuscript comparisons. Report the boundary and spacing statistics separately and check their sensitivity to certain versus uncertain separators.
open.question: Can a single fixed generation process reproduce within-line edge-glyph dependence, its discontinuity at line breaks, and the observed separator distribution jointly?

spec.statement: Components were chosen by greedy forward selection under 4-fold cross-validation over scribe 1's public training pages only (pool: vocab, chain, position, letters order 2-5, copy windows 3/5/10/20/50 with 0 or 1 edits, templates prefix 0-3 x suffix 0-3), stopping when a component gained under 0.002 bits per word. Cross-validated: 11.31 bits per word against 11.75 for the bag of words and 11.40 for glyph trigrams alone. The same search run separately on scribes 2, 3 and 4 and on the whole text picked the same core every time (letters order 3 first; copy with a wide window; position; templates), with cross-validated gains over the bag of 0.39, 0.39, 0.58 and 0.38 bits per word; scribe 5 has too few training words. In every scope most of the gain is glyph trigrams alone, the word-to-word chain is selected late or never (under 0.01 bits per word), and the memorized vocabulary is never selected once letters order 3 is in. Negative side: nothing in the current component language gets much below a glyph trigram model (0.04 to 0.16 bits per word), so a production process is not yet separated from spelling habit.
spec.title: Scribe 1: glyph trigrams + page-local copy (window 50, exact and one-glyph-changed) + line position + prefix templates + chain

detail.authors: Colin Layfield and Lisa Fagin Davis
established: Adjacent segments showed greater cosine similarity than shuffled segment orders in the manuscript and the comparison texts. The artificial self-citation text also produced this basic pattern, with a different score distribution.

The lowest five percent of sliding-window scores included many Herbal page boundaries and disproportionate Currier A-to-B transitions. The Biological, Pharmaceutical, Zodiac and Stars sections had relatively few scores below this cutoff.

open.check: Compare the full score distribution and the fraction of low scores at section and Currier transitions under identical preprocessing and matched block layouts.
open.question: Can a self-citation or other nonlinguistic process with prespecified changes at page and section boundaries reproduce the distribution of the manuscript's local similarities and transition scores?

detail.summary: The authors apply latent semantic analysis to short manuscript segments under three term-weighting schemes and compare adjacent with shuffled segment orders. A separate sliding-window analysis locates abrupt changes within the manuscript.
detail.title: The Application of Latent Semantic Analysis to the Voynich Manuscript
